claim: Lymphoid and myeloid cells are abundant in the tumor microenvironment.
source: Lymphoid and myeloid cells are abundant in the tumor microenvironment, can be quantified by immunohistochemistry and shape the disease course of human solid tumors.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract.

claim: Lymphoid and myeloid cells can be quantified by immunohistochemistry.
source: Lymphoid and myeloid cells are abundant in the tumor microenvironment, can be quantified by immunohistochemistry and shape the disease course of human solid tumors.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract.

claim: Lymphoid and myeloid cells shape the disease course of human solid tumors.
source: Lymphoid and myeloid cells are abundant in the tumor microenvironment, can be quantified by immunohistochemistry and shape the disease course of human solid tumors.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract.

claim: There is no comprehensive understanding of spatial immune infiltration patterns ('topography') across cancer entities and across various immune cell types.
source: Yet, there is no comprehensive understanding of spatial immune infiltration patterns ('topography') across cancer entities and across various immune cell types.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract.

claim: The study systematically measured the topography of multiple immune cell types in 965 histological tissue slides from N = 177 patients in a pan-cancer cohort.
source: In this study, we systematically measure the topography of multiple immune cell types in 965 histological tissue slides from N = 177 patients in a pan-cancer cohort.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and data collection performed in the study.

claim: The study provides a definition of inflamed ('hot'), non-inflamed ('cold') and immune excluded patterns.
source: We provide a definition of inflamed ('hot'), non-inflamed ('cold') and immune excluded patterns and investigate how these patterns differ between immune cell types and between cancer types.
evidence: This describes a key contribution of the study.

claim: Hot, cold and excluded topographies differ between immune cell types and between cancer types.
source: We provide a definition of inflamed ('hot'), non-inflamed ('cold') and immune excluded patterns and investigate how these patterns differ between immune cell types and between cancer types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's analysis.

claim: In an independent cohort of N = 287 colorectal cancer patients, hot, cold and excluded topographies for effector lymphocytes (CD8) and tumor-associated macrophages (CD163) alone are not prognostic.
source: In an independent cohort of N = 287 colorectal cancer patients, we show that hot, cold and excluded topographies for effector lymphocytes (CD8) and tumor-associated macrophages (CD163) alone are not prognostic, but that a bivariate classification system can stratify patients.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation cohort analysis.

claim: A bivariate classification system combining CD8 and CD163 topographies can stratify colorectal cancer patients.
source: In an independent cohort of N = 287 colorectal cancer patients, we show that hot, cold and excluded topographies for effector lymphocytes (CD8) and tumor-associated macrophages (CD163) alone are not prognostic, but that a bivariate classification system can stratify patients.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation cohort analysis.

claim: Malignant tumors growing in an immunocompetent host elicit an immune response, evident by the presence of various inflammatory/immune cell in tumor tissue.
source: Malignant tumors growing in an immunocompetent host elicit an immune response, evident by the presence of various inflammatory/immune cell in tumor tissue (Shalapour and Karin, 2015; Mantovani et al., 2008; Bindea et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tumor cells develop specific escape mechanisms against the immune system by manipulating inflammatory cells for their benefit.
source: In order to grow to a clinically relevant size, tumor cells develop specific escape mechanisms against the immune system by manipulating inflammatory cells for their benefit (de Visser et al., 2006; Dunn et al., 2002; Fridman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Tumor cells interfere with immune signaling, hijacking immunosuppressive cells and thereby shaping the immune infiltrate, which allows for tumor cell proliferation.
source: One of the key strategies is that tumor cells interfere with immune signaling, hijacking immunosuppressive cells and thereby shaping the immune infiltrate, which allows for tumor cell proliferation (Chen and Mellman, 2013; Chen and Mellman, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A number of immunotherapeutic drugs are currently available which interfere with immune cells in the tumor microenvironment in order to facilitate tumor control.
source: Currently a number of immunotherapeutic drugs are available which interfere with immune cells in the tumor microenvironment in order to facilitate tumor control (Becht et al., 2016a; Galluzzi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The complex nature of immune infiltrates impairs the development of more targeted approaches.
source: However, the complex nature of immune infiltrates impairs the development of more targeted approaches.
evidence: This is stated as a challenge in the field.

claim: Tailored combination treatments are widely proposed as a way to more effective cancer therapy.
source: Specifically, tailored combination treatments are widely proposed as a way to more effective cancer therapy (Sharma and Allison, 2015a; Sharma and Allison, 2015b; Zitvogel et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Systematically deciphering tumor-immune phenotypes is key to a better understanding and more effective tailoring of immunotherapies.
source: Systematically deciphering tumor-immune phenotypes is key to a better understanding and more effective tailoring of immunotherapies (Greenplate et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Analysis of solid tumor tissue slides by immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the gold standard to assess tumor immune infiltrate.
source: Analysis of solid tumor tissue slides by immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the gold standard to assess tumor immune infiltrate because it allows for exact quantification of type, density and localization of immune cells (Fridman et al., 2017; Becht et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: IHC allows for exact quantification of type, density and localization of immune cells.
source: Analysis of solid tumor tissue slides by immunohistochemistry (IHC) is the gold standard to assess tumor immune infiltrate because it allows for exact quantification of type, density and localization of immune cells (Fridman et al., 2017; Becht et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Digital pathology has been the method of choice to reliably and reproducibly analyze large cohorts of patient samples for more than a decade.
source: For more than a decade, digital pathology has been the method of choice to reliably and reproducibly analyze large cohorts of patient samples and can provide potential biomarkers for immunotherapy (Becht et al., 2016a; Kather et al., 2016; Gurcan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Digital pathology can provide potential biomarkers for immunotherapy.
source: For more than a decade, digital pathology has been the method of choice to reliably and reproducibly analyze large cohorts of patient samples and can provide potential biomarkers for immunotherapy (Becht et al., 2016a; Kather et al., 2016; Gurcan et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Immune cell quantification in digitized tissue has been used to identify robust and clinically relevant biomarkers in numerous cancer entities.
source: Immune cell quantification in digitized tissue has been used to identify robust and clinically relevant biomarkers in numerous cancer entities, for example in colorectal cancer (CRC) primary tumors and liver metastases (Galon et al., 2006; Halama et al., 2011; Mlecnik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Histological analysis of tumor-infiltrating lymphoid cells has been proven to be a reliable and prognostically relevant marker.
source: Histological analysis of tumor-infiltrating lymphoid cells has been proven to be a reliable and prognostically relevant marker (Galon et al., 2014; Denkert et al., 2016; International TILs Working Group 2014 et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antitumor immunity arises in a complex ecosystem of various cell types that closely interact with one another.
source: Antitumor immunity arises in a complex ecosystem of various cell types that closely interact with one another, such as effector lymphocytes (Li et al., 2016), macrophages (Halama et al., 2016; Biswas and Mantovani, 2010), dendritic cells (Gardner and Ruffell, 2016), granulocytes (Coffelt et al., 2016), innate lymphoid cells (Crome et al., 2017), regulatory T cells (Nishikawa and Sakaguchi, 2010), natural killer cells (Crome et al., 2013; Barrow and Colonna, 2017), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (Talmadge and Gabrilovich, 2013) and other cell types (Kather et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In tumor tissue, T lymphocytes (T cells) and macrophages are among the most abundant immune cells.
source: In tumor tissue, T lymphocytes (T cells) and macrophages are among the most abundant immune cells and are closely related to clinical outcome (Fridman et al., 2017; Kather et al., 2017; Fridman et al., 2012; Kather et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: T lymphocytes and macrophages are closely related to clinical outcome.
source: In tumor tissue, T lymphocytes (T cells) and macrophages are among the most abundant immune cells and are closely related to clinical outcome (Fridman et al., 2017; Kather et al., 2017; Fridman et al., 2012; Kather et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A paradigm for the classification of tumor-immune phenotypes has emerged with three classes of tumors: 'cold' tumors, 'immune-excluded' tumors, and 'hot' tumors.
source: After years of detailed IHC analysis of solid tumor slides, a paradigm for the classification of tumor-immune phenotypes has emerged and three classes of tumors are generally assumed: 'cold' tumors (or 'immune desert', showing no immune cell infiltration), 'immune-excluded' tumors (with immune cells aggregating at the tumor boundaries) and 'hot' tumors (or 'inflamed' tumors, showing pronounced immune infiltrates in the tumor core (Chen and Mellman, 2017; Lanitis et al., 2017; Joyce and Fearon, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 'Cold' tumors show no immune cell infiltration.
source: 'cold' tumors (or 'immune desert', showing no immune cell infiltration)
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: 'Immune-excluded' tumors have immune cells aggregating at the tumor boundaries.
source: 'immune-excluded' tumors (with immune cells aggregating at the tumor boundaries)
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text.

claim: 'Hot' tumors show pronounced immune infiltrates in the tumor core.
source: 'hot' tumors (or 'inflamed' tumors, showing pronounced immune infiltrates in the tumor core (Chen and Mellman, 2017; Lanitis et al., 2017; Joyce and Fearon, 2015).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the text with citations.

claim: The classification of tumors into cold/excluded/hot is generally accepted but backed by surprisingly little quantitative data.
source: However, although this classification is generally accepted, it is backed by surprisingly little quantitative data.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Fundamental biological questions regarding the cold/excluded/hot concept are essentially unanswered.
source: Fundamental biological questions regarding this concept are essentially unanswered, such as: Do these topographies exist in all tumor entities? Is there a difference between immunotherapy-sensitive and immunotherapy-insensitive tumor types? Does the concept of cold/excluded/hot apply to lymphoid and myeloid cells, or only to one of them? Do all tumors use the same strategies for immune escape?
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: Two recent studies of immunophenotypes in colorectal cancer (CRC) have shown that the average immune cell density is higher around the tumor than in the tumor core.
source: Two recent studies of immunophenotypes in colorectal cancer (CRC) have shown that the average immune cell density is higher around the tumor than in the tumor core (Bindea et al., 2013; Mlecnik et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The concept of cold/excluded/hot tumors was not investigated in previous CRC immunophenotype studies.
source: Yet, the concept of cold/excluded/hot tumors was not investigated in these studies.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in previous research.

claim: Other comprehensive studies have not taken spatial patterns of immune cell phenotypes into account.
source: Also, other comprehensive studies have not taken spatial patterns of immune cell phenotypes into account (Becht et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A previous study investigated spatial patterns of lymphoid and myeloid cells in human solid tumors using only tissue microarrays (TMA), precluding differentiation between invasive margin and tumor core.
source: Another previous study investigated spatial patterns of lymphoid and myeloid cells in human solid tumors – however, only tissue microarrays (TMA) were included in that study, precluding any possible differentiation between invasive margin and tumor core (Tsujikawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The study analyzed CD3+ T-lymphocytes, CD8+ T-lymphocytes, PD1+ T lymphocytes, FOXP3+ T lymphocytes, CD68+ monocytes/macrophages, and CD163+ monocytes/macrophages.
source: In particular, this included a systematic analysis of the following immune cells: CD3+ T-lymphocytes, CD8+ T-lymphocytes, PD1+ T lymphocytes, FOXP3+ T lymphocytes (which we assume to be largely 'regulatory', although the role of FOXP3 is more complex (Wang et al., 2007) and CD68+ and CD163+ monocytes/macrophages.
evidence: This describes the immune cell types analyzed in the study.

claim: FOXP3+ T lymphocytes are assumed to be largely 'regulatory', although the role of FOXP3 is more complex.
source: FOXP3+ T lymphocytes (which we assume to be largely 'regulatory', although the role of FOXP3 is more complex (Wang et al., 2007)
evidence: This is stated with a citation acknowledging complexity.

claim: Immune cell densities were measured in three spatial compartments per slide: outer invasive margin (0 – 500 µm outside the tumor invasion front), inner invasive margin (500 µm to the inside), and tumor core.
source: We measured immune cell densities (number of cells per mm², Figure 1A–B) in 965 immunostained histological tissue slides (listed in Supplementary file 3) in the pan-cancer cohort in three spatial compartments per slide (Figure 1C): outer invasive margin (0 – 500 µm outside the tumor invasion front), inner invasive margin (500 µm to the inside) and in the tumor core.
evidence: This describes the methodology with reference to figures.

claim: Colorectal adenocarcinoma primary tumors and liver metastases had a higher cell count in the outer invasive margin than in the tumor core.
source: In accordance with previous studies, colorectal adenocarcinoma primary tumors and liver metastases had a higher cell count in the outer invasive margin than in the tumor core (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to figures.

claim: Melanoma samples had higher cell counts in the inner tumor than outside of the tumor for all analyzed cell types.
source: Melanoma samples had higher cell counts in the inner tumor than outside of the tumor for all analyzed cell types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Using cell densities for CD3+ and CD8+ cells in all three spatial compartments, the majority of optimization runs converged on two clusters.
source: We used cell densities for CD3+ and CD8+ cells in all three spatial compartments and used multiple methods to determine the optimal number of clusters. For CD3 and CD8 separately as well as for both together, the majority of the optimization runs converged on two clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 4), mostly representing 'hot' and 'cold' tumors.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: There was no strong tendency to converge on three clusters in unsupervised clustering of lymphocyte densities.
source: There was no strong tendency to converge on three clusters, which means that there is no strong inherent grouping into 'hot', 'cold' and 'immune excluded' tumors.
evidence: This is a finding from the clustering analysis.

claim: There is a high correlation between 'tumor core' and 'inner invasive margin' cell densities.
source: We found that in general, there was a high correlation between 'tumor core' and 'inner invasive margin', but not between either compartment and the 'outer invasive margin' (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: There is not a high correlation between 'outer invasive margin' and either 'tumor core' or 'inner invasive margin' cell densities.
source: We found that in general, there was a high correlation between 'tumor core' and 'inner invasive margin', but not between either compartment and the 'outer invasive margin' (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the correlation analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: 'Tumor core' and 'inner invasive margin' can be collapsed into one compartment because cell counts in these compartments are highly correlated.
source: 'Tumor core' and 'inner invasive margin' can be collapsed into one compartment because cell counts in these compartments are highly correlated.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation analysis.

claim: High density outside of the tumor with a low density inside the tumor can be described as 'immune excluded'.
source: high density outside of the tumor with a low density inside the tumor can be described as 'immune excluded'.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the results.

claim: Low density inside and outside the tumor is 'cold'.
source: Low density inside and outside is 'cold'
evidence: This is a definition provided in the results.

claim: High density inside the tumor is 'hot' regardless of cell density outside of the tumor.
source: high density inside the tumor is 'hot' regardless of cell density outside of the tumor (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: This is a definition provided in the results with reference to figures.

claim: Different tumor types showed very different distributions of immune topographies.
source: Based on these definitions, different tumor types showed very different distributions of immune topographies (Figure 3A–F).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to figures.

claim: Tumor types that are to some degree sensitive to approved cancer immunotherapies (such as melanoma (MEL), lung adeno (LUAD), lung squamous (LUSC) and head and neck squamous (HNSC)) had a large proportion (approximately half) of CD3-hot, CD8-hot and PD1-hot tumors.
source: Most strikingly, tumor types that are to some degree sensitive to approved cancer immunotherapies (such as melanoma (MEL), lung adeno (LUAD), lung squamous (LUSC) and head and neck squamous (HNSC) had a large proportion (approximately half) of CD3-hot, CD8-hot and PD1-hot tumors.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Colorectal primary (COAD-PRI) and colorectal metastatic (COAD-MET) had a very high proportion of CD3-excluded tumors.
source: In accordance with previous studies (Halama et al., 2011), colorectal primary (COAD-PRI) and colorectal metastatic (COAD-MET) had a very high proportion of CD3-excluded tumors (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Differences between tumor types were most pronounced for regulatory T-cells (Foxp3+ cells).
source: Differences between tumor types were most pronounced for regulatory T-cells (Foxp3+ cells, Figure 3D)
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: More than half of lung adeno (LUAD), head and neck squamous (HNSC), stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) and esophageal (ESCA) cancer samples had Foxp3-hot topographies.
source: with more than half of lung adeno (LUAD), head and neck squamous (HNSC), stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD) and esophageal (ESCA) cancer samples having Foxp3-hot topographies.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Close to half of all analyzed COAD-PRI samples were Foxp3-hot.
source: Also, while close to half of all analyzed COAD-PRI samples were Foxp3-hot, the vast majority of all COAD-MET samples were Foxp3-cold (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: The vast majority of all COAD-MET samples were Foxp3-cold.
source: Also, while close to half of all analyzed COAD-PRI samples were Foxp3-hot, the vast majority of all COAD-MET samples were Foxp3-cold (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: Tumors often had different topographies for a pair of immune cell markers.
source: Indeed, we saw that tumors often had different topographies for a pair of immune cell markers (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: There was a discordance in a substantial number of cases that were lymphoid-hot and myeloid-cold.
source: Especially, regarding lymphocytic and myeloid markers, there was a discordance in a substantial number of cases that were lymphoid-hot and myeloid-cold (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: CD3 and CD8 topographies were mostly concordant.
source: CD3 and CD8 topographies were mostly concordant (Figure 5A) as can be expected because CD8+ lymphocytes are a subset of CD3+ lymphocytes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure and biological knowledge.

claim: CD8+ lymphocytes are a subset of CD3+ lymphocytes.
source: as can be expected because CD8+ lymphocytes are a subset of CD3+ lymphocytes.
evidence: This is stated as established biological knowledge.

claim: There was a notable discordance between CD8 and Tregs topographies.
source: Regarding CD8 vs. Tregs (Figure 5B), there was a notable discordance.
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: Most colorectal primary tumors (COAD-PRI) that were Foxp3-excluded were CD8-cold.
source: For example, most colorectal primary tumors (COAD-PRI) that were Foxp3-excluded were CD8-cold.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Several melanomas (MEL) that were CD68-hot were CD8-cold, which was rarely observed in other tumor types.
source: Analyzing tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) labeled with CD68 (Figure 5D), we found that several melanomas (MEL) that were CD68-hot were CD8-cold which was rarely observed in other tumor types.
evidence: This is a finding from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: Colorectal cancer liver metastases (COAD-MET) were mostly CD8-excluded, corresponding to a CD68-excluded or CD68-hot phenotype.
source: Colorectal cancer liver metastases (COAD-MET) were mostly CD8-excluded, corresponding to a CD68-excluded or CD68-hot phenotype.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Tumors of different immunophenotypes require different ways of immune escape.
source: These findings suggest that tumors of different immunophenotypes require different ways of immune escape and that these mechanisms can only be distinguished when considering a two-dimensional myeloid-lymphoid classification system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings.

claim: Immune escape mechanisms can only be distinguished when considering a two-dimensional myeloid-lymphoid classification system.
source: These findings suggest that tumors of different immunophenotypes require different ways of immune escape and that these mechanisms can only be distinguished when considering a two-dimensional myeloid-lymphoid classification system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings.

claim: Ovarian cancer (OV) was an outlier in hierarchical clustering due to its low infiltration with almost all immune cell subsets.
source: We found that ovarian cancer (OV) was an outlier (Figure 6H) due to its low infiltration with almost all immune cell subsets (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis with reference to figures.

claim: Highly immunogenic tumor types such as melanoma (MEL), stomach cancer (STAD) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC: LUAD and LUSC) were close in hierarchical clustering.
source: Highly immunogenic tumor types such as melanoma (MEL), stomach cancer (STAD) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC: LUAD and LUSC) were close in hierarchical clustering.
evidence: This is a finding from the hierarchical clustering analysis.

claim: Cell densities of CD8 and CD163 in the tumor core and the outer invasive margin were not significantly correlated to overall survival in the DACHS cohort.
source: Cell densities of CD8 and CD163 in the tumor core and the outer invasive margin were not significantly correlated to overall survival (hazard ratios [HR] for death from any cause were 1.00 for both cell types in both compartments, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis in the validation cohort.

claim: Bivariate immune topographies showed significant association to overall survival in the DACHS cohort.
source: However, bivariate immune topographies showed significant association to overall survival: With 'CD8-cold, CD163-cold' as a reference cohort, the HR was 1.75 for 'CD8-excluded, CD163 excluded' (p=0.041) and the HR was 2.71 for 'CD8-excluded, CD163-hot' (p=0.025, Supplementary file 6 and Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a finding from the survival analysis in the validation cohort with reference to a figure.

claim: With 'CD8-cold, CD163-cold' as a reference cohort, the HR was 1.75 for 'CD8-excluded, CD163 excluded' (p=0.041).
source: With 'CD8-cold, CD163-cold' as a reference cohort, the HR was 1.75 for 'CD8-excluded, CD163 excluded' (p=0.041)
evidence: This is a specific finding from the survival analysis.

claim: With 'CD8-cold, CD163-cold' as a reference cohort, the HR was 2.71 for 'CD8-excluded, CD163-hot' (p=0.025).
source: the HR was 2.71 for 'CD8-excluded, CD163-hot' (p=0.025, Supplementary file 6 and Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a specific finding from the survival analysis with reference to a figure.

claim: The tumor microenvironment is a highly complex, heterocellular ecosystem.
source: The tumor microenvironment is a highly complex, heterocellular ecosystem (Bindea et al., 2013; Tape, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Multiple immune cell types are involved in the tumor microenvironment and ultimately shift it towards a tumor-promoting or tumor-rejecting environment.
source: Multiple immune cell types are involved in this system and ultimately shift it towards a tumor-promoting or tumor-rejecting environment (Chen and Mellman, 2017; Fridman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Immune cells determine whether a tumor will be responsive to immunotherapy.
source: Also, these immune cells determine whether a tumor will be responsive to immunotherapy (Becht et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Immunotherapy outcomes vary pronouncedly between different tumor entities and between different patients within a given entity.
source: However, immunotherapy outcomes vary pronouncedly between different tumor entities and also between different patients within a given entity.

claim: The biological basis for differences in immunotherapy outcomes is still not entirely clear.
source: The biological basis for these differences has been the subject of various studies but is still not entirely clear.

claim: We currently lack a comprehensive classification system for multiple effector parts of the immune system.
source: Most importantly, we currently lack a comprehensive classification system for multiple effector parts of the immune system.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap.

claim: The study provides evidence for a classification of tumor-immune phenotypes into hot, cold and immune excluded spatial patterns.
source: In the present study, we have performed a large-scale systematic analysis of lymphoid and myeloid phenotypes of human solid tumors. We provide evidence for a classification of tumor-immune phenotypes into hot, cold and immune excluded spatial patterns.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: Hot, cold and immune excluded patterns can be detected not only in lymphocyte infiltrates but also in macrophage infiltrates.
source: These patterns can be detected not only in lymphocyte infiltrates (lymphoid classification, as previously assumed by most studies) but also in macrophage infiltrates (myeloid classification).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Lymphoid and myeloid patterns are not always identical and a two-dimensional classification is needed to accommodate all possible lymphoid-myeloid phenotypes.
source: Interestingly, lymphoid and myeloid patterns are not always identical and a two-dimensional classification is needed to accommodate all possible lymphoid-myeloid phenotypes.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Lymphoid-hot tumors are more prevalent in immunotherapy-responsive tumor entities such as melanoma and lung adenocarcinoma than in other entities such as colorectal cancer.
source: We found that lymphoid-hot tumors are more prevalent in immunotherapy-responsive tumor entities such as melanoma and lung adenocarcinoma than in other entities such as colorectal cancer.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Immune-excluded tumors are common in head and neck tumors (HNSC).
source: Immune-excluded tumors, such as lymphoid-excluded and myeloid-excluded tumors are common in head and neck tumors (HNSC).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Characteristic patterns of immune evasion (via T cell exhaustion or infiltration by Tregs) are not exclusive to specific tumor-immune phenotypes but can be detected across the defined categories.
source: Lastly, we show that characteristic patterns of immune evasion (via T cell exhaustion or infiltration by Tregs) are not exclusive to specific tumor-immune phenotypes but can be detected across the defined categories.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: High density of CD8+ cells in colorectal cancer is associated with long survival.
source: It has been previously shown that high density of CD8+ cells in COAD is associated with long survival (Galon et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: High density of CD163+ cells in colorectal cancer is associated with poor survival.
source: while high density of CD163+ cells is associated with poor survival (Fridman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Some large studies have shown only a very modest impact of CD8+ cell density on overall survival in colorectal cancer.
source: However, some large studies have shown only a very modest impact of CD8+cell density on overall survival (Glaire et al., 2018).

claim: In the DACHS cohort, CD8+ cell density alone and CD163+ cell density alone were not clearly associated with differences in overall survival.
source: Likewise, in the DACHS cohort which we analyzed as part of this study, CD8+ cell density alone and CD163+ cell density alone were not clearly associated with differences in overall survival.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation cohort analysis.

claim: For both CD8 and CD163, the immune topographies (cold, excluded, hot) were not associated with differences in overall survival in the DACHS cohort.
source: Also, for both cell types, the immune topographies (cold, excluded, hot) were not associated with such differences.
evidence: This is a finding from the validation cohort analysis.

source: However, classifying patients according to bivariate (CD8 combined with CD163) immune topographies identified statistically significant associations to survival in a multivariable statistical model (Figure 7D).

claim: For CD8-excluded tumors, CD163-cold, excluded and hot tumors had a significantly different prognosis (log rank p-value 0.019).
source: This was particularly clear for CD8-excluded tumors: in this case, CD163-cold, excluded and hot tumors had a significantly (log rank p-value 0.019) different prognosis (Figure 7E).

claim: A multivariate analysis of spatial distributions of multiple immune cell types may be superior to merely quantifying a particular type of immune cells in colorectal cancer and possibly other human solid tumors.
source: These findings suggest that a multivariate analysis of spatial distributions of multiple immune cell types may be superior to merely quantifying a particular type of immune cells in COAD and possibly other human solid tumors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings.

claim: The study adds a systematic approach to a hitherto subjective classification of tumor-immune phenotypes.
source: Our study adds a systematic approach to a hitherto subjective classification of tumor-immune phenotypes.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: The new classification could constitute a novel framework to investigate immunotherapy responsiveness in clinical trials.
source: This new classification could constitute a novel framework to investigate immunotherapy responsiveness in clinical trials.

claim: The classification sheds light on common immunological aspects by describing a shared immune topography across human solid tumors.
source: Also, this classification sheds light on common immunological aspects by describing a shared immune topography across human solid tumors.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's contribution.

claim: All experiments were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects (CIOMS), the Belmont Report and the U.S. Common Rule.
source: All experiments were conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, the International Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research Involving Human Subjects (CIOMS), the Belmont Report and the U.S. Common Rule.
evidence: This is stated in the ethics statement.

claim: Anonymized archival tissue samples were retrieved from the tissue bank of the National Center for Tumor diseases (NCT, Heidelberg, Germany).
source: Anonymized archival tissue samples were retrieved from the tissue bank of the National Center for Tumor diseases (NCT, Heidelberg, Germany) in accordance with the regulations of the tissue bank and the approval of the ethics committee of Heidelberg University (tissue bank decision numbers 2152 and 2154, granted to NH and JNK, ovarian cancer tissues granted to SS; informed consent was obtained from all patients as part of the NCT tissue bank protocol, ethics board approval S-207/2005, renewed on 20 Dec 2017).
evidence: This describes the source of tissue samples.

claim: Informed consent was obtained from all patients as part of the NCT tissue bank protocol.
source: informed consent was obtained from all patients as part of the NCT tissue bank protocol, ethics board approval S-207/2005, renewed on 20 Dec 2017
evidence: This is stated in the ethics statement.

claim: The study analyzed tissue samples of primary esophageal carcinoma (ESCA), primary gastric cancer (STAD), primary colorectal cancer (COAD-PRI), primary lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), primary lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), primary head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), primary bladder cancer (BLAC), ovarian cancer primary tumors (OV), melanoma primary tumors (MEL), and colorectal cancer liver metastases (COAD-MET).
source: We analyzed tissue samples of primary esophageal carcinoma (ESCA), primary gastric cancer (STAD), primary colorectal cancer (COAD-PRI), primary lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), primary lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC), primary head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSC), primary bladder cancer (BLAC), ovarian cancer primary tumors (OV) as well as melanoma primary tumors (MEL) and colorectal cancer liver metastases (COAD-MET).
evidence: This describes the tumor types analyzed in the study.

claim: The study acquired a set of N = 287 primary surgical specimen of colorectal adenocarcinoma from the DACHS study.
source: In addition to this pan-cancer cohort, we acquired a set of N = 287 primary surgical specimen of colorectal adenocarcinoma from the DACHS study (Hoffmeister et al., 2015; Brenner et al., 2011)
evidence: This describes the validation cohort with citations.

claim: Histological staining was performed for CD3, CD8, Foxp3, CD163, CD68, and PD1 on a Leica Bond automatic staining device using a hematoxylin-diaminobenzidine (DAB) staining protocol.
source: We performed histological staining for CD3 (dilution 1:100 with Leica antigen retrieval ER1 solution), CD8 (1:50 with ER1), Foxp3 (1:100 with Leica antigen retrieval ER2 solution), CD163 (1:500 with ER2), CD68 (1:2000 with Leica Fast Enzyme digestion) and PD1 (1:50 with ER1) on a Leica Bond automatic staining device using a hematoxylin-diaminobenzidine (DAB) staining protocol as described previously (Halama et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes the immunohistochemistry methodology with citation.

claim: For melanoma, FastRed was used as a chromogen.
source: For melanoma, FastRed (Leica #DS9390) was used as a chromogen.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail.

claim: Stained whole slide tissue sections were digitized.
source: Stained whole slide tissue sections were digitized as described previously (Halama et al., 2016).
evidence: This describes a methodological step with citation.

claim: Almost all samples were stained for six immune cell markers (CD3, CD8, Foxp3, CD163, CD68, PD1).
source: Almost all samples were stained for these six immune cell markers. In cases of insufficient tissue availability, only CD3, CD8 and CD163 staining was performed.
evidence: This describes the staining protocol.

claim: In cases of insufficient tissue availability, only CD3, CD8 and CD163 staining was performed.
source: In cases of insufficient tissue availability, only CD3, CD8 and CD163 staining was performed.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail.

claim: The image analysis pipeline included manual annotation of three regions of interest (ROI) in each histological whole slide image.
source: Our image analysis pipeline was composed of several steps: First, manual annotation of three regions of interest (ROI) in each histological whole slide image (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the image analysis methodology with reference to a figure.

claim: The ROIs were 'tumor core' (TU_CORE), 'inner invasive margin' (MARG_500_IN) and 'outer invasive margin' (MARG_500_OUT).
source: The ROIs were 'tumor core' (TU_CORE), 'inner invasive margin' (MARG_500_IN) and 'outer invasive margin' (MARG_500_OUT).
evidence: This describes the ROI definitions.

claim: Invasive margins were 500 µm wide.
source: Invasive margins were 500 µm wide.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail.

claim: All positively stained cells were automatically counted using the open source software QuPath.
source: Second, we automatically counted all positively stained cells using the open source software QuPath (Figure 1B) (Bankhead et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the cell counting methodology with citation and reference to a figure.

claim: Intensity thresholds and other parameters for cell detection and classification were set manually for each staining type and were identical for all samples in the pan-cancer cohort.
source: Intensity thresholds and other parameters for cell detection and classification were set manually for each staining type and were identical for all samples in the pan-cancer cohort.
evidence: This describes a methodological detail.

claim: All cell detection scripts were manually checked for plausibility in all tumor entities.
source: All cell detection scripts were manually checked for plausibility in all tumor entities.
evidence: This describes a quality control step.

claim: Cell density values were normalized by percentile within each staining type and were visualized as 'target plots'.
source: For all further analyses, cell density values were normalized by percentile within each staining type and were visualized as 'target plots' (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the data normalization and visualization method with reference to a figure.

claim: To ensure reproducibility, 60 tissue specimen were randomly selected and all analysis steps were repeated.
source: To ensure reproducibility of our digital pathology pipeline, we randomly selected 60 tissue specimen and repeated all analysis steps.
evidence: This describes a reproducibility experiment.

claim: There was a high correlation (Pearson's correlation coefficient was >0.74, p-value<0.001) between the original and replicate experiments.
source: There was a high correlation (Pearson's correlation coefficient was >0.74, p-value<0.001) between these replicates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the reproducibility experiment with reference to a figure.

claim: For negative control slides, very few cells were false positive (<<0.1%).
source: Furthermore, two slides that served as negative controls for CD3 and CD163 staining, 231/86516 (<<0.1%) and 1/38311 (<<0.1%) cells were false positive.
evidence: This is a finding from the negative control experiment.

claim: Three different methods for clustering were used: a gaussian mixture model, k-means and hierarchical clustering.
source: To determine the optimal number of clusters in this data set, we used three different methods for clustering: a gaussian mixture model, k-means and hierarchical clustering.
evidence: This describes the clustering methodology.

claim: For 1 up to 12 clusters, three loss functions were computed for each clustering approach, using the Davies-Bouldin, the Calinski-Harabasz or the silhouette criteria for quality of clustering.
source: For 1 up to 12 clusters, we computed three loss functions for each approach, using the Davies-Bouldin (Davies and Bouldin, 1979), the Calinski-Harabasz (CalińskiCalinski and Harabasz, 1974) or the silhouette (Rousseeuw, 1987) criteria for quality of clustering.
evidence: This describes the clustering methodology with citations.

claim: All image analysis steps were implemented in QuPath and all downstream analyses were implemented in MATLAB R2017a.
source: All image analysis steps were implemented in QuPath (see key resources) and all downstream analyses were implemented in MATLAB (Mathworks, Natick, MA, USA) R2017a.
evidence: This describes the software implementation.

claim: All experiments were run on a standard workstation (Intel i7 Processor, 8 cores, 32 GB RAM, Microsoft Windows 10.1).
source: All experiments were run on a standard workstation (Intel i7 Processor, 8 cores, 32 GB RAM, Microsoft Windows 10.1).
evidence: This describes the computational infrastructure.

claim: All source codes are released under an open access license.
source: We release all source codes under an open access license (Kather, 2018; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/immuneTopography).
evidence: This describes data availability.

claim: All raw data from the experiments are released.
source: Also, we release all raw data from our experiments (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This describes data availability.

claim: All survival analyses were performed in R version 3.5.1 using the packages survminer, survival, ggfortify and ggplot2.
source: All survival analyses were performed in R version 3.5.1 (R-project.org) using the packages survminer, survival, ggfortify and ggplot2.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis software.
